frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong bargaining power through pipeline and LNG exports, but European buyers are pressing for price flexibility and long-term supply assurances.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign energy technology
frictionVectors.details: International partners remain important for upstream investment and technical capacity, although Sonatrach preserves dominant control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain embedded in Angola's transport and energy infrastructure, constraining policy flexibility despite efforts to diversify creditors.

frictionVectors.title: Mature oil-sector decline
frictionVectors.details: Falling or volatile petroleum output pressures state revenues and increases reliance on foreign operators, while local-content reforms have produced uneven results.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and transit rupture
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger and regional sanctions have disrupted established transit routes and exposed Benin's dependence on cross-border trade and external political conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security corridor
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel threatens roads, communities, and prospective mining areas, increasing the cost of securing infrastructure near the northern frontier.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has increased its share of diamond value and marketing influence, but the partnership remains vulnerable to weak global demand and negotiations with De Beers.

frictionVectors.title: Commodity concentration
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on diamonds leaves national revenues exposed to price cycles, creating pressure to secure foreign investment in energy, logistics, and new minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and revenue from industrial gold operations, raising tensions with foreign investors over contracts, taxation, and operating security.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Growing reliance on Russian-linked security assistance expands Ouagadougou's strategic autonomy from Western partners but introduces new political, financial, and reputational dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control over nickel, rare-earth and gold projects, but weak institutions and opaque licensing leave room for foreign operators and illicit networks to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security friction
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over accusations of support to armed groups in eastern DRC, limiting regional cooperation and increasing dependence on shifting external security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its ports, airfields and maritime position among European, North American and Chinese partners, creating financing and alignment pressures around critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and limited maritime enforcement constrain national control over valuable waters, while climate stress raises the economic and food-security stakes.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports, the Chad-Cameroon pipeline and major transport projects remain dependent on foreign capital, contractors and security arrangements, limiting domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside instability near Nigeria and the Central African Republic, disrupts resource access and weakens state authority outside core administrative zones.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and Russian influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors retain major political and economic influence, particularly around gold and diamond sites, raising concerns that security assistance is being exchanged for opaque resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and border corridors
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and insecurity along routes to Cameroon and Sudan leave trade dependent on foreign-backed protection and informal networks, weakening the government's ability to regulate exports.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil production, foreign operators and export infrastructure, while weak transparency limits the public capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: External security balancing
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are recalibrating ties with France, Russia and regional partners as conflict in Sudan and instability across the Sahel strain border security, humanitarian capacity and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's continued administration of Mayotte constrains Comoros' territorial sovereignty and fuels recurring diplomatic tensions. The dispute also affects maritime boundaries, migration management, and access to surrounding resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence and Port Capacity
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, foreign aid, and imported energy, limiting policy autonomy. Weak port and transport infrastructure leaves strategic connectivity vulnerable to outside financiers and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: M23, Rwanda, and Border Security
frictionVectors.details: M23 territorial gains and persistent allegations of external backing continue to challenge Kinshasa's control in the east. The conflict disrupts mining zones, trade corridors, and civilian access to state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mineral Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain central to competition among Chinese, Western, and regional investors. Contract renegotiations and infrastructure-for-minerals arrangements offer revenue opportunities but leave the country exposed to opaque terms and limited local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state's fiscal and geopolitical leverage remains closely tied to offshore oil production and foreign energy operators. Price volatility and limited diversification constrain independent resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important to roads, ports, and urban infrastructure. These relationships improve connectivity while raising concerns over debt exposure, procurement transparency, and strategic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover Risk
frictionVectors.details: Instability from Burkina Faso and Mali continues to pressure northern border communities and security spending. Abidjan is strengthening regional partnerships, but attacks or militant infiltration could disrupt trade corridors and agricultural zones.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire retains strong state oversight of cocoa exports but captures a limited share of downstream value. European sustainability rules, multinational purchasing power, and volatile prices continue to constrain producer sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Great-Power Military Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti hosts major foreign military facilities, including Chinese, American, French, and other international deployments. The rents provide fiscal leverage but make national security and diplomatic room for maneuver dependent on competing external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port revenues and logistics infrastructure are vulnerable to Red Sea shipping disruptions and regional conflict. Heavy reliance on externally financed projects, particularly Chinese-linked infrastructure, creates repayment and strategic-control risks.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt refinancing and large investment inflows from Gulf partners and international lenders increase outside influence over strategic assets, including ports, logistics, and land development.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile allocation
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's dam operations remain a core national-security concern, with Egypt seeking binding guarantees on drought-year water flows and dispute resolution.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector decline and foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field output and dependence on international energy companies limit fiscal autonomy while the state seeks new offshore investment.

frictionVectors.title: Regional gas infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Gas monetization depends on cross-border supply and external technical capital, leaving domestic resource control exposed to market and partner-country pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral projects provide essential foreign exchange but rely on external operators, creating persistent disputes over labor, revenue sharing, and transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline sits amid rivalry involving Gulf states, Türkiye, Egypt, Ethiopia, and wider maritime actors, increasing pressure over ports and security access.

highlights: South African supply chains anchor economy

frictionVectors.title: External market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade access, electricity, fuel, and transport links remain heavily tied to South Africa and regional customs arrangements, constraining independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure financing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Road, energy, and industrial projects depend on external lenders and development partners, creating limited but persistent influence over national planning.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia's leverage over regional energy and water politics but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: External debt pressures and reliance on foreign capital for rail, telecoms, energy, and logistics projects can limit Addis Ababa's room to set wholly independent economic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The post-transition government is seeking greater state control over oil, manganese, and timber, but foreign operators remain central to production and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Railway Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on the Transgabon Railway constrains mineral expansion and exposes sovereignty goals to financing, maintenance, and operator decisions involving external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Casamance Spillover
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia remains strategically dependent on Senegal for regional security and transport access, limiting its room for independent external alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Fisheries Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, tourism, and fisheries activity generates revenue but leaves the country vulnerable to outside control over maritime assets and value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Galamsey Crisis
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining damages water systems and weakens state control, with domestic networks and foreign-linked trading channels capturing substantial value.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Terms
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking better terms in lithium, gold, and bauxite partnerships while fiscal pressure and IMF-linked reforms reduce negotiating flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea’s largest prospective resource project depends on foreign mining consortia, Chinese-linked infrastructure, and complex rail-and-port financing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Transition Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Military rule concentrates bargaining power over minerals but creates uncertainty over elections, contracts, and the durability of state commitments to outside investors.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Raw cashew exports dominate rural livelihoods, while foreign traders and processors capture much of the value because domestic processing and storage remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Border Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Maritime and fisheries issues involving Senegal, alongside weak port capacity, constrain Bissau’s ability to independently manage coastal resources and trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing IMF-linked fiscal reforms with major Chinese-financed infrastructure obligations. Debt-service pressure limits Nairobi's room to dictate terms on transport, energy, and digital infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in Lamu logistics and Kenya's emerging critical-mineral prospects is increasing. Nairobi faces pressure to convert investment into domestic processing, jobs, and stronger environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Water-export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue but reinforces dependence on South Africa as the dominant buyer and infrastructure partner. Delays, cost overruns, and disputes over compensation continue to test sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Hydropower and fiscal vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower offers diversification but remains exposed to drought, transmission constraints, and external financing conditions. Limited domestic industrial capacity reduces Lesotho's ability to capture more value from its water and energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore and gold concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining firms dominate capital-intensive iron-ore and gold operations, leaving Liberia exposed to commodity cycles and uneven local value capture. The government is under pressure to strengthen revenue enforcement, community benefits, and domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia and nearby logistics corridors attract competing foreign commercial and strategic interests. Liberia's infrastructure needs make it vulnerable to contracts that improve connectivity but constrain future policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest terminals, fields, and the National Oil Corporation's operating environment. Production disruptions and opaque revenue arrangements weaken national control over the primary strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: External military and security influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed security networks and contractors remain embedded in Libya's rival power structures. Their presence protects local enclaves and commercial interests while obstructing unified border, energy, and infrastructure governance.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral concentration
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining projects provide export earnings but expose Madagascar to price volatility, external ownership, and limited downstream processing. Fiscal renegotiation and local-content demands are likely to intensify as strategic-mineral competition grows.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridors and environmental pressure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, roads, and energy systems tied to mining projects can bypass broader national development priorities. Land disputes, water stress, and ecological damage continue to generate resistance around major extraction zones.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in uranium, graphite, and rare-earth projects while trying to strengthen licensing, local-content, and revenue safeguards. Limited negotiating leverage and fiscal pressure leave the state exposed to externally financed deals.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Recurring electricity shortages, fuel-import needs, and constrained transport corridors weaken economic sovereignty. Reliance on external lenders and neighboring ports increases exposure to infrastructure and balance-of-payments shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-Code Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is demanding larger state and domestic participation in gold mining, creating disputes with international operators and raising contract-enforcement concerns. Gold remains the fiscal backbone, but insecurity limits the state's ability to control production regions.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian security support has narrowed Western partnerships without eliminating militant threats. Sanctions history, conflict, and fragile transport infrastructure continue to restrict access to fuel, equipment, and export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Gas Development
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers Mauritania new export revenue and bargaining power, but offshore production remains dependent on foreign operators, technology, and regional coordination with Senegal. Delays or disputes over revenue-sharing could weaken expected gains.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports depend heavily on the SNIM railway and the port of Nouadhibou, leaving national revenue vulnerable to infrastructure outages and external financing conditions. Chinese and Gulf-linked investment is expanding options but may deepen strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Sovereignty and Base Politics
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos sovereignty process remains tied to the future of the Diego Garcia military facility and broader UK-US strategic interests. The issue directly affects Mauritius's maritime jurisdiction, seabed resources, and diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Imported Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control over its economy but remains dependent on imported fuel, food, and technology. Port modernization and renewable-energy projects require outside capital, creating competition among Indian, Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco exercises effective control over much of Western Sahara and is developing fisheries, phosphates, renewables, and ports there, while the territory's status remains internationally contested. Legal challenges and rival diplomacy can affect investment and export access.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Security
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's industrial expansion is constrained by drought, groundwater stress, and continued exposure to imported energy and strategic technologies. Desalination, renewables, and green-hydrogen projects improve resilience but require substantial foreign finance and partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led LNG projects remain exposed to Islamist insurgency, requiring substantial external security support. This limits Maputo's control over project timelines and operating conditions.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Revenue and Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International operators and lenders retain significant influence over gas development, while weak institutions and public debt constrain Mozambique's bargaining power over future revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of New Energy Assets
frictionVectors.details: International firms are positioning for offshore oil, green hydrogen, uranium, and critical minerals. Namibia is strengthening local-content and state-participation tools, but financing and technology needs preserve substantial outside leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Export-Corridor Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, water, and power bottlenecks could limit sovereign value capture from new projects. Regional logistics partnerships are necessary but may dilute domestic control over infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Oil Contract Rebalancing
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is seeking greater state control over uranium and oil assets while revisiting foreign contracts. Political rupture with Western partners raises operational, legal, and investment risks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reduced Western involvement has increased reliance on Russian security ties and regional partners. This may strengthen regime autonomy but does not solve insurgency, transport, or export-capacity constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Pipeline Exposure
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain important to offshore production, technology, and financing, while theft, sabotage, and weak pipeline security reduce national capture of hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Dangote and State Refining Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining capacity could reduce dependence on imported fuel, but regulatory disputes, crude-supply constraints, and market concentration create new contests over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and mineral-trading role face sustained international scrutiny over alleged links to armed groups and supply chains originating in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Development finance, technology partnerships, and security relationships strengthen Rwanda's state capacity but give outside actors leverage over infrastructure, minerals, and regional diplomatic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe relies heavily on foreign capital and technical expertise to assess disputed or underexplored offshore blocks. Weak bargaining leverage could limit future state control over petroleum revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea security
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on regional and external naval cooperation to protect its maritime domain. Limited patrol capacity leaves fisheries, shipping, and any future offshore energy assets vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New hydrocarbon production has intensified demands for greater national participation, transparency, and domestic value creation. Rebalancing agreements with international operators risks slowing investment or triggering legal disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors and Gulf, European, and Asian partners are competing for influence over ports, logistics, and transport corridors. Dakar's strategic role creates leverage but also exposes the country to dependency on external financing and operators.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on external naval and surveillance support to protect its vast maritime zone from piracy, illegal fishing, and trafficking. Security cooperation can strengthen sovereignty while narrowing strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign investment concentration
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, fisheries, property, and infrastructure remain exposed to foreign capital and external demand. Concentrated ownership and climate vulnerability can reduce domestic control over key economic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports and fiscal expectations, but foreign operators retain substantial influence over financing, logistics, and marketing. Commodity-price swings and limited domestic processing constrain sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external partners are important sources of infrastructure finance and construction capacity. Projects can close major development gaps but may increase long-term dependence through debt, procurement, or concession terms.

highlights: Ports sit at a strategic crossroads

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime access competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other external actors compete for influence over Somali ports, security partnerships, and Red Sea access. Fragmented federal authority makes it difficult to secure consistent national terms for strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource governance
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries attract foreign interest while federal, state, and private authorities contest licensing and revenue control. Weak enforcement capacity raises risks of opaque contracts, illegal fishing, and unequal benefit sharing.

highlights: Grid and logistics remain binding constraints

frictionVectors.title: Power-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity and transmission weaknesses constrain industrial sovereignty and expose the country to external financing and technology providers. Efforts to diversify generation are advancing but remain vulnerable to delays and cost pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Competition among China, the United States, Europe, and Gulf investors for platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains is increasing. Pretoria retains policy leverage but faces pressure to provide stable export access and investment terms.

frictionVectors.title: Oil corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's export economy depends on pipelines and terminals crossing Sudan, leaving production and public revenue exposed to Sudan's conflict and foreign-linked operators. Disruptions directly threaten fiscal stability and sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and external patronage
frictionVectors.details: Political competition remains tied to control of oil revenues, security networks, and cross-border trade. Regional mediation and donor support are essential, but they also limit Juba's policy autonomy.

highlights: Gold and ports draw rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector capture
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling provide financing for armed actors while attracting competing regional and international networks. Weak state control prevents the sector from generating reliable public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, military facilities, and logistics corridors on the Red Sea are increasingly linked to the interests of Gulf, regional, and wider external powers. The civil war makes infrastructure concessions especially vulnerable to coercion and renegotiation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor concessions
frictionVectors.details: Investment in Dar es Salaam and regional transport corridors can strengthen Tanzania's trade sovereignty, but long-term concessions create concerns over strategic control and transparency. Competition among Gulf, Chinese, and Western-linked investors is intensifying.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking more local processing and state participation in minerals, including graphite and nickel. The challenge is converting foreign capital and technology into domestic value without discouraging investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major commercial and transshipment hub, but its strategic value gives foreign shipping, finance, and logistics interests substantial leverage. Concentration of trade infrastructure creates exposure to external market and security shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and illicit trafficking pressures from the Sahel are testing northern border security and diverting state resources. External security assistance is expanding, creating a sovereignty trade-off between protection and dependence.

frictionVectors.title: European Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia depends heavily on European trade, financing, and migration cooperation, giving the EU substantial influence over domestic economic and border policy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and fiscal constraints leave Tunisia reliant on imported hydrocarbons and vulnerable to external price shocks and infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline strengthens export capacity but remains politically contentious because of environmental, land, financing, and foreign-operator concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and contractors remain important in transport and energy infrastructure, creating repayment and strategic-dependence risks despite Uganda's efforts to diversify partners.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic value capture from copper while relying on multinational capital and foreign technical expertise to expand mines and processing.

frictionVectors.title: Export Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Copper exports depend on rail and port corridors through neighboring states, leaving national revenue exposed to regional transport disruptions and competing external infrastructure interests.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium Processing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is restricting unprocessed mineral exports to capture more value, but Chinese and other foreign investors retain strong leverage over mining finance, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, electricity shortages, and sanctions-related financing barriers weaken the state's ability to regulate mining operations and retain resource revenues.
